title: Coordinate liquid cooling and thermal ride-through
lead: Battery minutes do not create cooling minutes. Start with the manuscript’s mixed-cooling rack, then move to a separately labelled facility thermal model. The visual goal is to make both heat paths and their shared rejection boundary visible, so that the learner never mistakes a liquid-cooled label for complete removal of room heat.
objectives: Calculate liquid capture and residual air-cooling demand.
Use a sensible heat balance with declared fluid properties.
Compare a lumped thermal interval with electrical storage and restoration time.

sections.title: Keep heat and electrical input separate
sections.body: Cooling electricity is not thermal-removal capacity. For a sensible single-phase balance, heat rate = mass flow × specific heat × temperature rise, or density × volumetric flow × specific heat × rise. The illustrative 20 MW room balance requires about 1,381.98 m³/s air at density 1.2 kg/m³, specific heat 1,005 J/(kg K) and a 12 K rise. This aggregate balance does not specify a complete plant.

sections.title: Expose the heat that liquid cooling leaves behind
sections.body: At a 100 kW rack and an illustrative 80% liquid capture, the liquid path removes 80 kW and the air path still handles 20 kW. With water specific heat 4,180 J/(kg K) and a 10 K rise, liquid flow is about 1.914 kg/s. Under the stated air assumptions, residual airflow is about 1.382 m³/s. Direct-to-chip, rear-door and immersion arrangements have different interfaces and auxiliary dependencies; do not merge them into one universal loop.

sections.title: Start the thermal clock
sections.body: In a lumped loss-of-cooling model, temperature-rise rate is net heat input divided by effective thermal capacitance. With 150 MJ/K capacitance, 20 MW heat input, zero heat removal and a 5 K permissible rise, the interval is 37.5 s. Only thermally coupled mass on this time scale belongs in that capacitance, and local hot spots may reach limits sooner. A ten-minute UPS therefore does not establish ten minutes of thermal continuity.

challenge.question: How much room heat remains at the new rack boundary?
challenge.answer: 30 kW remains. This rack change does not silently change the separately declared 20 MW facility transient or its 37.5 s limit.

instructions: Read the declared boundary and units. Predict the selected result before calculating.
Run the starting case and inspect the ledger, assumptions and model limits.
Apply the challenge, run again, and explain the difference. Export only the last completed inputs and results.

scene.title: Two heat paths, two continuity clocks
storyboard: Reveal a rack cutaway, cold plates, residual air path and CDU.
Split the 100 kW heat balance into labelled 80 kW liquid and 20 kW air.
Move to the separately labelled 20 MW facility model and interrupt heat removal.
Run a physical-time cursor against the 37.5 s thermal limit and a separately stated 600 s electrical interval.
scene.interaction: Control capture fraction, rack power and restore time separately. Pause/scrub the labelled transient; show instantaneous full restoration only as an added preview assumption.
scene.staticAlternative: Heat-path table, flow calculations and temperature-rise-versus-time table with explicit assumptions.

assessments.question: Find water mass flow for 500 kW with an 8 K rise and specific heat 4,180 J/(kg K).
Derive the lumped thermal interval and identify a non-conservative case.
assessments.answer: Integrate constant net heat input: t = C_eff ΔT / Q. Local concentration, poor mixing or overestimated coupled mass can shorten the true interval.
assessments.rubric: State constant load, lost heat removal and spatial averaging.

assessments.question: Find residual room heat at 120 kW and 75% liquid capture.
assessments.rubric: Do not remove the residual air path from the diagram.

limits: Not CFD, local junction-temperature prediction, heat-exchanger design or selected-equipment qualification.
Fluid properties and thermal capacitance are illustrative, not site measurements.
